headline: All 12 findings of the admin-data audit were reproduced; none is refuted, four are corrected (AD-2, AD-7, AD-8, AD-9), and none argues for removing, hiding or merging a feature. The admin's lists, streaming and cache tags are well made. The waste is in the shell and the two home screens, and it is cost per owner tab and per save, so it multiplies with stores and owners, not with data. Production's 60 stores and 102 orders are the team's own testing, so nothing here is slow today and no saving is claimed for today. Measured again in this session: building the store menu takes 100 to 125 ms of blocking CPU per shell render (60 ms for a website, 243 ms for a store that is not open, 0.1 ms once the lookup is memoised). The shell is rendered in full on each hard load, after each save (599 refresh() sites in 176 files) and on each progress poll tick, but not on a soft navigation between pages of one store. A store Home view runs 29 to 46 statements before its first content, one of them thrown away. The products list runs 16 or more statements for an editor and uses 4. About 75 KB of the Home's 106 KB of page data is words and menu, re-sent on each redraw. The one argument that rested on empty tables (AD-2) is rewritten as cost that should follow use. Before opening is the cheap time to fix the shell and to add a per-screen statement budget, since nothing counts this today.

clean: Orders list: keyset paging at 50 rows (order-limits.ts:14), a count capped at 10,000 (order-limits.ts:16), named columns, the list behind Suspense, and a server-drawn view so its words are not sent whole (22 of 124 long strings of the orders area are in the measured document).
The store itself is read through 'use cache' with a per-store tag and an hours life (stores.ts:217-219); the admin does not re-read it per request.

Guard reads are shared inside one request with React cache(): readSession, getAccount, loadMembership (auth.ts:120, 214, 354). A page and its Suspense children calling requirePermission twice cost one read.
The member's row is read on every request on purpose (auth.ts:323-327, a security decision is never stale). Nothing here proposes caching it.

A soft navigation between pages of one store does not render the shell again: Next skips layouts the browser already holds (walk-tree-with-flight-router-state.js:65-70). The shell's cost is paid on hard loads, saves and refreshes only.
The store Home streams its six secondary cards behind Suspense (drafts, today, move watch, failed alerts, analytics alerts, briefing offer).
The AI manager's panel loads its chat and starts its conversation only when opened (ai-manager-launcher.tsx:105-127); the account menu's rows mount only while the menu is open (admin-menus.tsx:217).
Saving colours, the scheme or Basic and Advanced writes one row and does not redraw the page (account/actions.ts:82-100). Saving the language redraws once, as it must (admin-text.tsx:79-91).
No save revalidates a whole layout by path: revalidatePath is called 4 times in 2 files, each for one page.
Basic and Advanced (D454) is a client switch over the menu and hub cards; it does not make pages compute hidden cards.
The cached Store object is not handed whole to client components by admin pages: 12 of the receiving components were re-checked here and all are server components.
Plan limits are memoised per instance for a minute (limits.ts:24-47), so the Home's limits read is often free.
Cron health on the platform home is one statement over commerce.cron_jobs (cron-runs.ts:122-124).

No feature in this dimension is unused code paying a running cost for nobody: every read found serves a screen. The findings are about how often and how much, not about whether the feature should exist.

findings.title: The store menu is rebuilt with 220 slow permission lookups on every shell render
findings.evidence: matchPath() filters the 416-page table and sorts the 264 store pages on every call, and the sort runs a regex twice per comparison (pageParams). The layout calls storeTabs() and storeAreas(); each walks all 110 menu items through canOpenPath() -> permissionOfPath() -> matchPath(). Re-measured in this session in Node 22 after warm-up, three repeats: 121 to 125 ms with every feature on, 101 to 112 ms with the shop only, 60 ms for a website, 243 ms for a store that is not open (two lookups per item, layout.tsx:82). One matchPath() call is 0.46 to 0.53 ms; the filter and sort alone are 0.46 ms. With the lookup memoised by path the whole build is 0.1 ms. The answer depends only on the code and the member's keys. The shell is rendered on a hard load, after every save that calls refresh() (599 sites) and on every router.refresh(), not on a soft navigation (Next source read, see metrics).
findings.cost: 100 to 125 ms of blocking CPU per store shell render for a shop, 60 ms for a website, 243 ms for a suspended or closed store (measured on this machine). 64 ms more on the Settings and Website hub pages (measured: one storeSections() pass). About 130 ms per pass when the AI manager filters the 264 store pages (estimate: 264 times the measured 0.5 ms). It is synchronous, so the instance serves nothing else meanwhile. Today only the team pays it. It multiplies with every owner's saves once stores open (estimate: 1,000 saves cost about 2 minutes of CPU).
findings.who_pays: The server per shell render (function CPU), and the owner, who waits for it on every hard load, every save and every progress poll tick.
findings.fix: In admin-map.ts sort the pages per area once at module load and reuse them. In permissions.ts keep permissionOfPath() results in a Map keyed by path and access (the page table is static). Optionally call storeSections() once in the layout and derive tabs and areas from it.
findings.saving: Measured here: 100 to 125 ms down to 0.1 ms per shell render, 64 ms per hub page, and about 130 ms per AI manager pass (the last an estimate). On Vercel the figures will differ with its CPU; the same order is an estimate.
findings.risk: Low. Pure functions over a static table, covered by admin-map.test.ts, store-nav.test.ts and the permissions baseline. The memo must be keyed on path and access only, never on the member.
findings.already_tracked: no (searched docs for matchPath, permissionOfPath, storeTabs, storeAreas: no step or rule names this cost)
findings.verify_note: Opened every cited line. Wrote my own benchmark (skeptic-ad/nav.mjs) with the layout's exact canOpen and got 121-125, 101-112 and 60 ms against the auditor's 129, 115 and 67: same order, a few per cent lower. Added two figures the auditor did not time: 243 ms for a store that is not open, and 64 ms for one hub pass. Confirmed in Next's source that a save with refresh() renders every layout and that a soft navigation does not, so 'per shell render' is the right unit, not 'per navigation'. Nothing in this finding rests on unused features.

findings.title: The store Home runs 29 or more statements before it shows anything, one of them for nothing
findings.evidence: controlCenter() runs 1 statement, then 20 in one Promise.all (23 with Work on), then per-store reads for the threshold watch (1 to 4) and plan limits (0 to 11; the limits themselves are memoised for a minute per instance). The setup checklist adds 6 and demo content 1. The AI usage read (line 161) is used only by the owner's control center (owner page line 76); the store Home never reads center.ai, so that statement is thrown away on every Home view. Each feature added one count to this screen (drafts, order changes twice, payment terms, reviews, privacy, returns, books, hand-over), and every store runs all of them on every Home view whether or not it uses the feature. The file's own comment (lines 52-53) says 'never per store', yet lines 290-303 read per store. The pool holds 5 connections per instance (client.ts:67), so the batch goes through in about six rounds and takes the instance's whole pool meanwhile. The checklist's 6 reads run even when every step is done. store_billing is read 3 or 4 times on one hard load (layout, checklist, control center, limits when not memoised).
findings.cost: 29 to 46 statements held before the page's first content; on the owner's control center the per-store part grows by 1 to 15 statements per store. Not timed. Today's rows are the team's test data, so the statements are fast; the count per view is what multiplies with owners.
findings.who_pays: The database and the server per Home view; the owner waits for all of it before Home's header and figures appear.
findings.fix: 1) Do not read AI usage when onlyStore is set. 2) Draw the header, the week's figures and latest orders first, and move 'Needs your attention' and the checklist into their own Suspense sections, as the page already does for six others. 3) Fold the count-only attention reads into one statement that returns one row per store (the books read at lines 246-258 already does this with sub-selects), so a new feature adds a column, not a round trip. 4) Read the threshold watch and limits set-based for all stores, as the file's rule says. 5) Where a feature has a switch (reviews, books, Work), skip its read when the store has it off, so cost follows use.
findings.saving: Estimate: first content after about 8 statements instead of 29 or more; about 20 fewer statements per Home view once the counts are one statement; the owner's control center stops growing per store. One statement per Home view is saved for certain by step 1.
findings.risk: Medium-low. The attention list appears a moment after the header. The merged statement must keep each figure's permission rule (a figure only for a store where the member holds the key, lines 80-97).
findings.verify_note: Opened control-center.ts whole, setup.ts, usage.ts, limits.ts, turnover-watch.ts and the five attention helpers, and counted again: 1 + 20 + 1 + 1 + 6 + 1 = 30 for an owner of a shop, 29 when the limits memo is warm (the auditor missed limits.ts:24-47), up to 46. The thrown-away AI usage read is real: rg for 'center.' in the store page shows only center.stores and center.latest. Removed the auditor's argument that six reads hit tables 'that have never held a row': the platform is not open yet, so empty tables say nothing. What stands is that every store pays every feature's count on every Home view, and that one statement is discarded. Reworded fix 5 as cost following use, not as a feature being unwanted.

findings.title: Every admin request from a session without two-step calls Supabase Auth
findings.evidence: readSession() verifies the token, reads the account row, then for an aal1 session calls supabase.auth.getUser() over HTTP to list factors, on every request (React's cache spans one request only). Every page render, server action, notice poll and admin route handler goes through it. The writes that follow run only on a mismatch (the display mirror out of step, once) or while the break-glass switch is on, so in the steady state there are none.
findings.cost: One extra HTTP round trip per admin request for every account without a second factor, including each 60-second notice poll. Not timed here; the code review rates it severity 2. It grows with every owner who signs in without two-step once stores open.
findings.who_pays: The server per request and the owner on every navigation and save.
findings.fix: As the review says: use accounts.two_step_since as the fast path, or keep the factors answer five minutes per user and clear it on enrol and remove; move the writes into after().
findings.saving: One HTTP call per admin request for sessions without two-step (estimate: tens of milliseconds each; not measured).
findings.risk: Security-sensitive: the cached answer must be cleared when a factor is added or removed, and the platform's team must still be held at the second step.
findings.verify_note: Read auth.ts:100-176 and the code review's lines 110, 274 and 478. The call and its place hold. One nuance added: the 'up to two writes' fire only on a mismatch or with the kill switch on, not on an ordinary request, so the title no longer says 'and may write'. Already a step of the code review; it is listed here only so the plan does not count it twice.

findings.title: The store shell reads one thing after another, and checks Stripe set-up on every render
findings.evidence: The layout awaits the member, then the account's stores (used at top level for one footer link, line 151), then the support count, then the trial pause, each after the last; the account menu then awaits the Kaizen Life link with no Suspense. Next's guide says a top-level await in a layout holds the whole segment, children included. The only boundary above is the gate's (gated/layout.tsx:22-26), so the person sees the waiting screen until all are done; the page's own loading.tsx sits inside the frame. On every render the layout also schedules ensureTestAccount() and ensureStorePaymentMethods() with after(): one statement each, and a Stripe API call per render while a Kaizen-made test account is not yet active (connect.ts:270-275). The second looks for payment methods added to the platform, which changes only at a deploy; checkout runs the same check (checkout.ts:1516).
findings.cost: 5 database round trips in a row before the frame can paint on a hard load, and 2 statements (sometimes a Stripe call) after every shell render, which includes every save and every poll tick. New stores start in test mode (D20), so every new store's first minutes in the admin are the Stripe-call case.
findings.who_pays: The owner on each hard load and save; the server and database per shell render; Stripe's API quota in the not-yet-ready case.
findings.fix: Run the stores, support count, starter and trial reads in one Promise.all (they depend only on the member). Stream the Support badge, the banners and the Kaizen Life link behind Suspense. Keep 'test account ready' with the cached store (refresh the store's tag when the status is saved) and skip the after() when true. Move the payment-methods check to the Payments settings page and the existing payments job as one set-based statement; checkout keeps its own check.
findings.saving: Estimate: 3 fewer sequential waits before the frame paints, and 2 fewer statements per shell render for every active selling store.
findings.risk: Low. D20's promise (test purchases work without set-up) holds as long as a store whose test account is missing or not ready still runs the check. D23's text says the methods are asked for 'when the store's admin is opened or a checkout starts'; moving the admin half to the Payments page and a job changes its letter, so the decision's row needs a line.
findings.verify_note: Read the layout whole, the gate, admin-shell-parts.tsx, connect.ts:250-285 and 530-550, store-trial.ts:63-70, the rule in docs/rules/admin/commerce.md:60-64 and D20 and D23 in docs/decisions.md. The order of awaits and the two after() calls are as stated. Added what the auditor did not weigh: D23 names the admin as one of the two places the check runs, so the fix needs a note in the decision; checkout already runs the same check, so nothing is lost.

findings.title: Every save and poll re-sends 51 to 66 KB of unchanged shell words and menu
findings.evidence: Layouts hand whole catalogue areas to client components as props. Re-measured as JSON: common+setup+shell 20.4 KB (7.0 KB gzip); the assistant area 13.7 KB in English and 24.9 KB in Norwegian, sent for every owner though the panel is closed until pressed; the menu's tabs and areas 16.9 to 19.5 KB, each page address present three times (3 copies counted in the measured document). No client component reads the setup area (0 matches for useAdminText("setup"), and the context has no other reader), so its 6.9 KB is dead in every payload. The Home hands the whole home area (23.7 KB) to serve one streamed card, and the products list the whole products area (26.8 KB). Checked against a real document: in m/html/admin-home.html every long string of setup, assistant and home is present, and the handed words and menu are about 75 KB of the 106 KB of page data. A redraw after refresh() serialises all layouts again.
findings.cost: 51 to 54 KB (English) or 63 to 66 KB (Norwegian) of JSON per shell redraw for a store owner, about 14.5 to 18 KB gzipped; 24 to 27 KB more per view on Home and Products. Server time to serialise and browser time to parse and reconcile it, on every save and poll tick.
findings.who_pays: The owner's browser and the server per shell render.
findings.fix: Drop 'setup' from the gate's provider. Split the assistant area: hand the launcher only the words its closed button and badge use, and hand the chat's words down with the chat it already loads on open (through an AdminTextScope, not the English fallback). Hand a card its own slice (for example home.drafts), not the area. Send each menu address once and derive the tab's 'also' list in the client.
findings.saving: Estimate from the measured parts: 6.9 KB (setup) plus 12 to 23 KB (assistant) plus about 7.5 KB (menu addresses) less JSON per shell redraw, roughly half; in gzip terms about 8 to 11 KB, since the repeated addresses compress well. About 20 KB less JSON on each Home and Products view.
findings.risk: Low to medium. D540 makes a missing area a fault: e2e/signed-in/admin-text-fallbacks.spec.ts fails when a part reads an area nothing handed down, and its rule is to hand the area down where the part is drawn. So the chat's words must arrive in a scope with the chat, and the area must be split in the catalogue's types first.
findings.already_tracked: Partly: PSI PERF-01 (open) cut the admin's shared scripts (D540, 10-11 November); the words re-sent as props on each redraw are not in it
findings.verify_note: Re-measured every size with my own script (skeptic-ad/words.mjs): 20.4, 13.7 / 24.9, 23.7 and 26.8 KB match the auditor's within 0.4 KB; the menu is 16.9 to 19.5 KB depending on features and slug length. Added a second proof the auditor did not have: the measured Home document contains every string of the three areas, and words plus menu are about 70% of its page data, so confidence is raised from medium to high. Corrected the saving to say what it is after compression, and added the D540 test and rule that shape the fix.

findings.title: The platform Home holds its first paint for 18 statements and reads whole lists to show a number
findings.evidence: The page awaits five loaders in one Promise.all with no Suspense (0 matches in the file). platformOverview() calls listPlans() (3 statements with per-plan and per-price sub-counts and the Stripe sync table) to show plans.length, and usageRows() (a grouped join over ai_usage with prices, accounts and stores) to show two totals. planAnalytics(30) returns one row per store's plan and every plan move of the period and sums them in code. Pending access requests are counted four times on a hard load: layout line 67, the level switcher's own cached copy, the overview and the snapshot. Two definitions are in use: platform.ts:208 leaves out unconfirmed self-serve requests, the overview and the snapshot do not, so the tab's badge and the Home's figure can disagree.
findings.cost: 18 statements before the page paints and 6 or 7 in the layout; 4 of them count the same thing. Only the platform's own team opens this page, so the total is small; the plan lines grow by one row per store per view once stores sign up.
findings.who_pays: The platform's team on each visit; the database.
findings.fix: Count plans with one count(*). Sum AI requests and failures in one aggregate without the joins. Use one pendingRequests() behind React cache() everywhere, with one definition. Sum plan lines in SQL. Put the month's figures and the 'last 7 days' section behind Suspense so the attention list paints first.
findings.saving: Estimate: 18 statements to about 11, and the attention list after about 5.
findings.risk: Low. Choosing one definition of 'waiting' changes one of the two numbers shown today.
findings.verify_note: Opened all ten places and counted: overview 7, cron 1, snapshot 8, briefing setting 1, failed webhooks 1 = 18. The four counts of pending requests and the two definitions are in the code as stated. Dropped the auditor's production row count for ai_usage as an argument (it is the team's own testing); the join is oversize whatever the table holds. Marked as low priority: few people ever load this page, so it should come after the store shell and Home.

findings.title: The products list reads the whole editor context and a per-product check it does not need
findings.evidence: For a member who may edit, the list calls getEditorContext(): 10 statements in one batch (economic operators, two location reads, terms, the VAT matrix, booking staff, places, hosts, layouts, VAT categories), then 3 more one after another while the object is built (the store's AI provider, shipping profiles, market price rules; lines 198-200), and one more when the store uses the platform's AI key under a limit. The page uses terms and three fields of markets that are already in the cached store (lines 105-106). ratesNow() calls commerce.vat_rate() for every country and category and the result is dropped. productsNeedingMeasure() returns titles, categories (a recursive query) and SKUs for every active product that passes commerce.unit_price_required(), a function call per product, while the default view uses only the count (line 115).
findings.cost: 12 or more unused statements per products-list view for editors, 3 of them sequential after the batch, one a function call per country and category; one function call per active product per view for a notice's number. The list streams in only when the slowest chain is done.
findings.who_pays: The database and the server per view; the owner waits for the context's four rounds before the list appears.
findings.fix: Call listTerms() alone and take markets from the store. For the notice use a count (or exists) and read the rows only when ?needs=unit-price is asked; skip it when no category of the store requires a unit price.
findings.saving: Estimate: 16 or more statements down to 4 per view for an editor (products, the notice's count, terms, import jobs), and three sequential waits gone.
findings.risk: Low. The bulk panel needs only terms and markets (lines 105-106).
findings.already_tracked: no (the list's missing paging is code review step 1.13, see AD-10)
findings.verify_note: Read products.ts:100-200. The auditor counted the 10 statements of the Promise.all and missed the three awaits inside the returned object (aiFor, profileChoices, marketPriceRules), which run in sequence after it. So the context is 13 statements or more, not 10; the list is 16 or more, not 15; and 12 or more are unused, not 9. The finding is stronger than written and the same fix removes all of them.

findings.title: An account's memberships are read two to four times per request, in four shapes
findings.evidence: listStores(), ownerDesks(), booksMemberships() and controlCenter()'s first statement each join store_members to stores (three also to store_roles) for the same account with slightly different columns and filters. The owner layout awaits them one after another (stores, desks, domains for a non-owner, books clients, support count: 4 or 5 sequential awaits), and the owner's Stores page calls listStores() directly instead of the cached storesOf(), so the layout's read is repeated. In a store, the member row and the stores list are read on every hard load, and the control center reads the same membership a third time on Home.
findings.cost: 2 near-identical statements per store hard load, 3 on the store Home, 4 on the owner's home, and 4 or 5 sequential waits before the owner level's frame paints.
findings.who_pays: The database and the server per request; the owner on each hard load of /admin.
findings.fix: One membershipsOf(account) behind React cache() that returns slug, name, status, role, kind, role permissions, time zone and the Work, starter and sandbox flags; derive the stores list, the desks, the books clients and the control center's store list from it. Keep memberRow() separate, as its rule requires. Run the remaining layout reads together. Make the Stores page use storesOf().
findings.saving: Estimate: 2 to 3 statements and 2 to 3 sequential waits per owner-level hard load; 1 statement on the Stores page for certain.
findings.risk: Medium-low. Each caller filters differently (ownerDesks keeps closed stores and some starters; the others drop closed, starter and sandbox stores), so the shared read must carry the fields and each caller keeps its own filter.
findings.verify_note: Opened the four readers and the owner layout. The four shapes and the sequential awaits are real. The scope was too wide: 'three in a store' holds only on the store Home, where controlCenter() runs; any other store page reads the membership twice. Title, cost and the membership metric now say two to four. The saving is small next to AD-1 and AD-2; it is a true duplicate and worth doing with AD-2, not before.

findings.title: Progress polls redraw the whole admin, and a notice poll runs in every visible owner tab
findings.evidence: RefreshWhile calls router.refresh() every 5 s (cookie scan), 6 s (Dream Factory, three places), 10 s (page jobs, legal writing), 15 s (pack pictures, its own copy) or 20 s (domains), and does not stop when the tab is hidden; LiveRefresh does. Next's refresh re-fetches dynamic data 'including in shared layouts' (refresh-reducer.js), so each tick pays the whole shell of AD-1, AD-4 and AD-5 plus the page. The Dream Factory run is where a new store's owner lands first (store page.tsx:43-46), so this is the first screen most new owners will watch. Separately, the AI manager's button asks the notices feed every 60 s in every owner's tab while it is shown: the route reads the account, looks up the store by slug, runs the list query with limit 1 and discards it, then counts.
findings.cost: During a Dream Factory run: 10 full shell-and-page renders a minute per watching tab, hidden or not, each with the 100 to 125 ms menu build. Always: 60 requests an hour per visible owner tab, 4 statements each, one discarded, plus an Auth call for a session without two-step (AD-3). Estimate at 1,000 owners with a tab in view: 1,000 requests and 4,000 statements a minute for a badge.
findings.who_pays: The server per request and the database; the owner's browser re-parsing the shell each tick.
findings.fix: Give RefreshWhile and PackPicturesWatch the visibility check LiveRefresh has. For job progress, ask a small action for the job's state (the pattern store-drafts.tsx:39-45 already uses; an action that does not refresh sends no page back) and refresh once when it finishes. In the feed, answer count=1 with the count statement alone and take the store's id from what the layout already knows. Consider a longer poll when nothing was unread last time.
findings.saving: Estimate: a progress tick drops from the whole route to 2 or 3 statements; the notice poll from 4 statements to 2.
findings.risk: Low. A progress view must still redraw once when the job ends.
findings.verify_note: Opened every cited file. Two small errors fixed: the poll's constant is in src/lib/assistant-notices.ts:13, not 'ai-notices.ts:13', and the notice poll runs only while the tab is visible (ai-notices.tsx:41-43), so it is per visible tab, not per open tab. RefreshWhile itself has no such check, as stated. Counted the feed's statements again: account, store by slug, list, count = 4, the list thrown away when count=1. Added that the Dream Factory poll is the onboarding screen, which is why it matters at opening, and confirmed in Next's source that an action without refresh() returns no page.

findings.title: Three lists load everything; the customers list also groups every order before it cuts to 100
findings.evidence: listAdminProducts() has no limit and runs correlated sub-selects per product (picture, two variant counts, stock, title fallback, price range, and a vat_rate() call); every row is serialised to a client component (products-bulk.tsx is 'use client'). The platform's Stores list reads every store with billing. listCustomers() builds its rows from a CTE over every order of the store, grouped by email, and only then keeps 100 (line 177), so paging the result will not bound the work.
findings.cost: Per view: 6 sub-selects and a function call per product, and one pass over all of a store's orders. Today's catalogues and orders are the team's demo data, so nothing shows; the cost grows with each real store's catalogue and order history from the day it sells.
findings.who_pays: The database, and the owner's browser for the products table.
findings.fix: The review's step: one ListSearch and Pager, a page size on products, customers and stores. In addition, page the customers query by email before the aggregates, or keep per-customer totals, so the cut happens first.
findings.saving: Bounds the three views at a fixed page as stores grow (estimate; nothing to measure on demo data). Cheapest to do before opening, while no owner's bulk habits depend on the whole list being on one page.
findings.risk: Low. Bulk 'select all matching' on products needs the server-side pattern the orders list has.
findings.already_tracked: code review step 1.13 (FS2): Open; step 2.10 (FS9): Open. The customers aggregate over all orders is not written there
findings.verify_note: Read products.ts:305-348, customer-admin.ts:131-177 and the platform Stores page; read FS2, FS9 and steps 1.13 and 2.10 in the code review. All as stated, and already tracked except the customers aggregate. Rewrote the cost so it does not lean on '60 stores and 102 orders': those are test rows, and the point is what a real catalogue will cost, not that today is fine.

findings.title: The orders list re-reads store facts it already holds and waits in a row for the count
findings.evidence: loadOrderListContext() runs two statements, one after the other, for the store's time zone, market codes and currency rates; all three are in the cached Store the page already holds (store.timeZone, store.allMarkets, and the currencies with their rates read at stores.ts:241-242), and 'today' can be worked out in code. listOrdersPage() then reads rows, tags, the page before and the count one after another, though the count does not depend on the rows.
findings.cost: 2 statements and 3 to 4 sequential waits per orders-list view, out of 9 to 11 statements. The orders list will be the most opened admin page of a selling store.
findings.who_pays: The server per request; the owner waits a little longer for the list to stream in.
findings.fix: Build the context from the Store. Start the count together with the rows.
findings.saving: Estimate: 2 statements and 2 sequential waits per view.
findings.risk: Low. Rates read from a store cached for hours could lag a rate change for the sort-by-total key; refresh the store's tag when rates are saved, including by the daily rates job (not checked here whether it does).
findings.verify_note: Read order-list.ts:36-62 and 176-224, the orders page and stores.ts:239-242. The two statements and the sequential count are there, and the cached store does carry the currency rates. I did not check whether the job that updates rates refreshes the store's tag, so that stays a named risk and confidence stays medium.

findings.title: Nothing counts what a screen costs the server, so the Home grew to 30 statements unseen
findings.evidence: The admin has budgets for scripts (seven screens in admin-scripts.spec.ts) and ratchets for unchecked reads, but no count of statements or server time per screen. A search of src and docs for a statement or query budget, a per-request counter or Server-Timing found none (the only AsyncLocalStorage is actor.ts). control-center.ts states its own rule ('a handful of queries, never per store') in a comment and has since grown to 21 statements plus per-store reads, with nothing to notice it. The admin's speed beacon reports TTFB, which with a static shell says nothing about the data behind it. With no real traffic yet, production's statistics cannot show it either.
findings.cost: No running cost of its own. It is why AD-1, AD-2, AD-6 and AD-7 were not seen: each feature added one more read to a shared screen.
findings.who_pays: Everyone later: the owner in wait, the database in load, the team in audits like this one.
findings.fix: Count statements per request in db() (an AsyncLocalStorage counter) and log one line per admin render with the count and the time. Add an integration test that holds the shell, the store Home, the orders list, the products list and the platform Home to a number, lowered like the existing ratchet. Add the menu build to a unit test with a ceiling on lookups (a count, not a time, so it does not flake).
findings.saving: Keeps the savings of the findings above; no direct saving. Before opening it also gives the first real numbers per screen.
findings.risk: Low. The counter must not log statement text or values (the logging rule D400).
findings.already_tracked: no (code review step 4.6 'Measure, then tune' is Open and is about how people use Basic and Advanced, not a statement budget)
findings.verify_note: Repeated the search for any budget or counter (Server-Timing, statement or query budget, queryCount, AsyncLocalStorage) and read step 4.6's text at line 503: it measures usability, not server work. The comment in control-center.ts and the per-store reads below it are as quoted. Changed one detail of the fix: hold the menu build to a count of lookups rather than a time ceiling, which would flake on a busy CI machine.
